faqs.a: Business loans commonly include term loans with fixed payments, SBA-backed loans with lower rates, lines of credit for flexible drawing, and equipment financing secured by the asset. This calculator models the fixed-payment term loan.
faqs.q: What types of business loans exist?

faqs.a: Lenders look at business revenue, time in business, credit history and collateral. A clear plan for how the borrowed money generates returns strengthens any application.
faqs.q: How do I qualify for a business loan?

faqs.a: Interest on business loans is generally tax-deductible as a business expense in many countries, which lowers the effective cost. Confirm the rules with a tax professional in your jurisdiction.
Compare the loan's total interest against the profit the investment is expected to generate, and make sure monthly payments fit comfortably in cash flow even in a slow month.
faqs.q: How do I know if a loan is worth it?

faqs.a: Term loans are usually the cheapest for a fixed, known purchase. Lines of credit suit ongoing working-capital needs but often carry higher rates. Match the loan type to the use.
faqs.q: Term loan or line of credit?

faqs.a: Many business loans allow early repayment, sometimes with a prepayment penalty. Paying early saves interest, so check the agreement before you rely on it.
faqs.q: Can I repay a business loan early?

business-loan-calculator.formula:
monthly_payment = P x r x (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
r = annual_rate / 12, n = years x 12
total_interest = payment x n - P
howTo: Enter the loan amount your business needs.
Enter the annual interest rate offered.
Enter the repayment term in years.
Read the monthly payment, total repaid and total interest.
Compare against the expected return from the investment.
keyFacts: A business term loan provides a lump sum repaid in fixed monthly installments.
Lenders price business loans on revenue, credit history, collateral and time in business.
Interest on business borrowing is often tax-deductible as a business expense.
Shorter terms mean higher payments but less total interest.
The monthly payment must fit comfortably in the business's cash flow, not just on paper.
